answer: Each identity carves one timber hull joint for a test voyage, its 14 notch depths set by a sonnet sequence seeded from its key and hash-committed before cutting. A lab loads the joint to failure and admits it only if the break load matches the pre-committed simulation within 8%. One joint takes 5 skilled hours and $18 of timber; 1,000 Sybils need 5,000 hours, $18,000 in wood and $35 lab fees each, and copied joints fail because their seed pattern differs. Trade-off: agents without workshop access are excluded and lab throughput caps admission at 40 per day.
